title: Impact of preoperative intervention for smoking cessation on postoperative length of stay and cost for spine surgery patients: Propensity score matching analysis
summary: Preoperative smoking cessation interventions significantly reduce the length of stay (LOS) and hospitalization costs for spine surgery patients. A retrospective study at a Tokyo hospital analyzed 317 spine surgery patients who smoked, comparing 262 who received smoking cessation interventions against 55 who did not. Using propensity score matching to control for various variables, it was found that the intervention group had a significantly shorter postoperative LOS by about 10 days and a cost reduction of over 1.5 million yen. The study concluded that preoperative smoking cessation effectively lowers postoperative complications, LOS, and overall hospitalization costs, underscoring the importance of such interventions in clinical settings, especially in countries like Japan where the aging population is rising.

title: Does timing matter? The effect of preoperative smoking cessation on the risk of infection or revision following rotator cuff repair
summary: This study investigates the impact of smoking cessation on postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing rotator cuff repair (RCR). Using a national database of over 120 million health records, the study identifies patients based on smoking status: never smokers, current smokers, and former smokers with varying cessation periods before surgery. The primary outcomes analyzed were infection and reoperation rates at 90 days, 1 year, and 2 years post-surgery. Results indicate that current smokers and those who quit smoking less than 6 months before surgery have higher risks of both reoperation and infection compared to never smokers. Notably, former smokers who ceased smoking more than 6 months before surgery did not exhibit increased risks of postoperative complications. The study emphasizes the transient nature of smoking-related risks and supports the recommendation for smoking cessation well in advance of operative procedures. Limitations include potential data biases and lack of controlled measures for variables like rotator cuff tear size and pack-years of smoking. The findings underscore the importance of preoperative smoking cessation to mitigate surgical risks.

title: Impact of smoking cessation on healing after foot and ankle surgery
summary: A historical cohort study investigated the impact of smoking cessation on wound healing after elective foot and ankle surgery by comparing three groups: patients who quit smoking before surgery, former smokers, and nonsmokers. The study involved 265 patients who underwent surgery performed by a single surgeon, examining factors such as age, BMI, diabetes, and smoking status. Compliance to smoking cessation was high, and no significant difference in wound healing complications was found between the groups, though those who ceased smoking preoperatively showed similar healing outcomes to nonsmokers and former smokers. The study highlighted that preoperative smoking cessation reduces wound healing risks comparable to those who never smoked, though the small sample size and lack of an active smoking comparison group were limitations. Further studies with larger sample sizes and active smoker groups are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Impact of Nicotine Replacement Therapy on Breast Surgery Outcomes
summary: This study evaluated the impact of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) on postoperative outcomes for patients undergoing breast surgery. Conducted via a retrospective chart review within the Yale New Haven Health System from 2014 to 2020, the research included 613 breast procedures with 17.2% of patients using NRT. Comparison between NRT users and non-users covered documented smoking status, surgical type, and complications like infection, wound dehiscence, and tissue necrosis. Multivariable logistic regression highlighted that NRT use was not a significant predictor of postoperative complications. Instead, factors like procedure type, increased body mass index (BMI), and age were more influential on complications. Overall, this study suggests that NRT does not elevate risks of postoperative complications in breast surgery patients, recommending that surgical preparation focus more on managing BMI and smoking cessation rather than the potential unverified risks of NRT.

title: What Is the Fate of Total Joint Arthroplasty Patients Who Are Asked to Quit Smoking Prior to Surgery?
summary: The study assessed the effects of smoking cessation amongst primary total joint arthroplasty (TJA) patients who were asked to quit smoking prior to surgery, examining cessation success and subsequent perioperative outcomes. The retrospective review included data from 2008 to 2020, involving 101 survey respondents from a single academic medical center. Findings indicated that 62% of patients successfully quit smoking before surgery, and of those, 51% remained smoke-free six months postoperatively. Notably, patients who did not quit smoking exhibited significantly higher wound complication rates (27%) compared to those who did quit (5%). This underscores the importance of smoking cessation for reducing surgical risks and improving outcomes. Despite challenges in the process, the study advocates for standardized smoking cessation protocols in orthopedic practice to enhance both surgical and long-term health outcomes. Limitations include self-reported data and varied surgeon documentation practices.

title: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy use during index hospital admission following cystectomy for bladder cancer: A retrospective cohort study
summary: The study aimed to examine the use of smoking cessation pharmacotherapy (SCP) in patients undergoing cystectomy for bladder cancer, utilizing the Premier Healthcare Database. Out of 21,624 patients, 3,676 current smokers were identified, representing an estimated 16,063 admissions. Only 27.9% of these patients received SCP, mostly nicotine replacement therapy. Factors like older age, black race, and certain comorbidities influenced SCP receipt. Hospital characteristics, including size and teaching status, did not significantly affect SCP rates. The study found no association between SCP receipt and hospital length of stay or 90-day readmission and mortality rates. The findings indicate a substantial gap in providing evidence-based smoking cessation care post-surgery, highlighting an opportunity to enhance urologic oncology care through targeted interventions and standardization.
